lmsArticle.title: System Design HLD Example: Distributed Cache Platform
lmsArticle.subtitle: Interview HLD for a distributed cache with eviction, invalidation, and resilience trade-offs.
lmsArticle.excerpt: Distributed caches trade strict consistency for sub-millisecond read latency, using consistent hashing to scale horizontally without causing database-shattering "cache stampedes" during cluster rebalancing.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

Distributed caches trade strict consistency for sub-millisecond read latency, using consistent hashing to scale horizontally without causing database-shattering "cache stampedes" during cluster rebalancing.

Instagram's primary database once served user profile reads at 28,000 QPS until a single viral post triggered a "cache miss storm." This storm drove the database to 95% CPU utilization in seconds, threatening to…

This walkthrough focuses on **Distributed Cache: Use Cases & Requirements**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- A distributed cache is an in-memory, key-value store shared across multiple servers.
- Functional Requirements - Standard Operations : Support GET(key) , SET(key, value, TTL) , and DELETE(key) .
- - TTL (Time-To-Live) : Support per-key expiration to ensure data doesn't stay stale forever.

**Concepts in play:** caching, system-design-hld-architectures, consistency-replication, hash-tables-and-bloom-filters

## Stage 1 — Basics: Baseline Architecture

- In a distributed environment, the "Cache" is not one server, but a cluster of servers.
- Cache Client : A library integrated into the application that handles the logic of where to find a key.
- Cache Nodes : Independent servers (like Redis or Memcached instances) that store data in RAM.
- Consistency Mechanism : Logic to ensure that when a database record is updated, the corresponding cache entry is invalidated or updated.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Basics: Baseline Architecture - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant",
    "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** Consistency Mechanism : Logic to ensure that when a database record is updated, the corresponding cache entry is invalidated or updated.

## Stage 2 — Mechanics: Key Logic

- Consistent Hashing The core challenge is: Which node stores key "user:123"?
- - Naive approach : hash(key) % N .
- If you add a node (N becomes N+1), almost every key's location changes.
- This causes a 100% cache miss rate — a "Cache Stampede." - Consistent Hashing : Keys and nodes are mapped onto a logical circle (the "Ring").

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** This causes a 100% cache miss rate — a "Cache Stampede." - Consistent Hashing : Keys and nodes are mapped onto a logical circle (the "Ring").

## Stage 3 — Estimations & Design Goals

- - QPS : 10M reads/sec, 1M writes/sec.
- - Storage : 100 nodes 128GB RAM = 12.8TB total capacity.
- - Object Size : Average 2KB per object.
- A 1% drop in hit rate at 10M QPS adds 100,000 queries per second to the database.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** A 1% drop in hit rate at 10M QPS adds 100,000 queries per second to the database.

## Stage 4 — High-Level Design

- architecture { "version": 1, "title": "High-Level Design - Subsystem Overview", "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.", "view": "high-level", "patte…
- The application checks the Cache Client Library first; the library hashes the key and consults the Consistent Hash Ring to determine which physical node owns that key.
- On a miss (step 6), the application queries the database directly, and the result is written back to the owning cache node (step 8).
- This backfill ensures that subsequent reads for the same key are served from cache without touching the database.

*Applies **hash-tables-and-bloom-filters** to the decision above.*

```mermaid

```

```

graph LR
    App[Application Service] -->|1. Get Key| Client[Cache Client Library]
    Client -->|2. Hash Key| Ring((Consistent Hash Ring))
    Ring -->|3. Route| NodeA[Node A]
    Ring -->|4. Route| NodeB[Node B]
    Ring -->|5. Route| NodeC[Node C]
    
    App -->|6. Miss| DB[(Database)]
    DB -->|7. Backfill| Client
    Client -->|8. Set Key| NodeA
```

**Observable outcome:** This backfill ensures that subsequent reads for the same key are served from cache without touching the database.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Consistent Hashing Ring Internals and LRU Eviction Performance Under Scale

- Two mechanisms dominate the engineering complexity of a distributed cache: determining which node owns a key without causing re-hashing storms when topology changes, and deciding which keys to evict when RAM is full whi…
- Internals: The Consistent Hash Ring and Virtual Nodes Naive modulo sharding — hash(key) % N — has a fatal flaw: when the node count N changes by even 1, almost every key's owning node changes.
- At 10M QPS this produces a complete cache miss storm for tens of seconds, hammering the database to destruction.
- Consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a conceptual ring using a hash function.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a conceptual ring using a hash function.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Cache Strategies: How Twitter, Facebook, and Netflix Use Distributed Caches

- Twitter's Twemproxy is a lightweight cache proxy that sits between application servers and Redis/Memcached instances.
- Twemproxy handles consistent hashing, connection multiplexing, and automatic failover transparently from the application.
- The key insight Twitter solved was connection fan-out: 10,000 application server threads each opening direct connections to 100 cache nodes creates 1,000,000 concurrent connections.
- Twemproxy reduces this to 100 connections from the proxy pool.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Twemproxy reduces this to 100 connections from the proxy pool.

## End-to-end outcome

A distributed cache is an in-memory, key-value store shared across multiple servers.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Redis vs. Memcached and Choosing the Right Cache Pattern

The most common interview mistake is proposing Write-Through caching for all workloads.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs and Failure Modes in Distributed Cache Design

- **Detection:** Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a popular key expires, dozens or thousands of simultaneous requests all miss the cache and hit the database concurrently.
- **User or operator impact:** Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a popular key expires, dozens or thousands of simultaneous requests all miss the cache and hit the database concurrently.

### Lessons Learned from Cache Failures at Scale

- **Detection:** The Stampede That Took Down Instagram's Database.
- **User or operator impact:** The Stampede That Took Down Instagram's Database.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
